project.name: blog
project.description: A terminal/REPL-styled developer portfolio built on the Next.js App Router with React 19 and Tailwind CSS v4. It exposes a command-driven UI (help/about/experience/projects/contact/lab/theme) backed by a command catalog and resolver in lib/commands/, plus canvas-based easter eggs and lab experiments (matrix-rain, glitch banner, DVD bounce, shatter/crash fragment explosion, gravity-well particle solver, raymarched black hole). Ships as a static export to GitHub Pages, with a Vitest + Testing Library suite covering the terminal, effects, and hooks.

nodes.name: globals.css
nodes.summary: Global stylesheet (503 lines) defining the terminal/REPL portfolio aesthetic with Tailwind v4 directives, CSS custom properties for the theme palette (e.g. --primary), and styling for terminal chrome, scrollbars, and effects.

nodes.name: layout.tsx

nodes.name: SimpleIcon

nodes.name: portfolio.tsx

Exports a default Portfolio named component. Heavy useEffect/useCallback/useState usage.

nodes.name: ScrollbackLog

nodes.name: pdf-window.tsx

tour.title: Project Overview: A Portfolio That Is a REPL
tour.description: Start with the README, the project's own story. This is not a traditional portfolio page — the whole site behaves like a terminal: you type `help` and get commands (about, experience, projects, contact, lab, theme, ...). It is built on Next.js (App Router), React 19, and Tailwind v4, and ships as a static export to GitHub Pages. package.json confirms the exact stack and scripts: Next.js 16, React 19.2, Vitest + Testing Library for tests. Read both files to anchor everything that follows.
tour.languageLesson: A 'static export' means every page is pre-rendered to plain HTML/JS at build time — no server at runtime. That is why this single-page app can deploy to GitHub Pages.

tour.title: App Shell: From Route to Terminal
tour.description: Trace the Next.js App Router entry points. layout.tsx defines the document shell — metadata, viewport, and the <html>/<body> wrapper that imports the global styles. page.tsx is the single root route of the site: it renders the Portfolio terminal inside a FragmentExplosionProvider. next.config.mjs is where the static-export decision lives (`output: 'export'`), plus unoptimized images and a pinned Turbopack root. This is the whole routing surface: one page, one shell.
tour.languageLesson: In Next.js App Router, `layout.tsx` persists across routes while `page.tsx` is route-specific. With `output: 'export'` there is no server runtime — the layout and page are rendered at build time.

tour.title: The Terminal Aesthetic: Global Styles and Design Tokens
tour.description: The REPL look comes from globals.css: Tailwind v4 directives, CSS custom properties for the theme palette (e.g. --primary), and styling for terminal chrome, scrollbars, and effects. Themes are cycled by swapping these custom properties, so the whole page recolors without touching component styles. lib/utils.ts exports `cn`, a className merge helper (clsx + Tailwind twMerge) used everywhere to compose conditional classes safely.
tour.languageLesson: CSS custom properties (variables) are the backbone of theming: components read var(--primary) at render time, so changing the variable recolors every consumer instantly.

tour.title: UI Primitives: Icons and ASCII Banners
tour.description: Before the terminal itself, look at the smallest building blocks. simple-icon.tsx renders SVG icons with optional title/className, merging classes via `cn`. ascii-banner.tsx renders the ASCII 'regis' figlet art from lib/ascii-art.ts and decorates it with a glitch effect. These two primitives show the design system's two visual languages: crisp SVG glyphs and chunky terminal ASCII art.
tour.languageLesson: Separating 'art data' (ascii-art.ts: plain string arrays) from 'art renderer' (ascii-banner.tsx: React component) lets tests and other consumers reuse the art without mounting components.

tour.title: The REPL Hub: portfolio.tsx
tour.description: This is the heart of the project and the biggest fan-in node. portfolio.tsx implements the interactive REPL: it manages the command input, renders the scrollback log, mounts the content sections, wires the RunCommandProvider context, and coordinates the easter-egg hooks. Nearly everything on the page is a section or effect that this component decides to show based on what the user types. Understand this file and you understand the site's choreography.
tour.languageLesson: This is a 'smart container' pattern: portfolio.tsx holds state and orchestration while delegating visual details to dumb presentational children (scrollback-log, sections).

tour.title: Input and Output: TerminalInput and ScrollbackLog
tour.description: The two workhorses of the terminal surface. terminal-input.tsx handles submission and editing UX: up/down arrow history navigation, tab completion sourced from the command catalog, a shake-on-error animation for unknown commands, and focus management. scrollback-log.tsx displays the output lines with auto-scroll behavior, tracking container resizes via ResizeObserver. Together they turn a div into something that feels like a real shell.
tour.languageLesson: Tab completion is data-driven: the input field asks the command catalog for completions rather than hardcoding them, so new commands automatically become tab-completable.

tour.title: The Command System: Catalog, Resolver, Session
tour.description: The site's 'brain'. catalog.ts is the fan-in hub exporting TAB_COMPLETE_COMMANDS, section aliases, and static command responses. resolver.ts exposes getStaticResponse, which normalizes a typed command and delegates to the right handler. session.ts adds stateless helpers — shuffling and popping 'secret' commands so easter eggs don't repeat immediately. This three-file pipeline is what maps `help`, `about`, or a hidden trigger to something rendered in the scrollback.
tour.languageLesson: Separation of concerns in a command pipeline: catalog = data (what commands exist), resolver = logic (how input maps to output), session = state helpers (avoiding immediate repeats). Pure functions make this trivially unit-testable.

tour.title: Domain Types and the Theme System
tour.description: lib/types.ts is tiny but central: it exports THEMES, a readonly list of themes used for cycling and validation. Because the command system and the UI both depend on it, this module is a dependency hub — change the theme list here and the `theme` command, the type checks, and the CSS variables all stay in sync. It is the contract between the command layer and the rendering layer.
tour.languageLesson: A small, dependency-free types module is a cheap way to share a domain contract (which themes exist) across command logic and UI without creating circular imports.

tour.title: Content Sections: What the Commands Reveal
tour.description: The sections are the actual portfolio content. section-map.ts exports SECTION_COMPONENTS, mapping section keys (typed by lib/types) to React components — the translation layer that turns a `projects`-style command into a scroll target. about.tsx has a typewriter phrase cycle and runnable command links; experience.tsx renders expandable role cards with tech tags and can open a PDF presentation window (pdf-window.tsx, an accessible focus-trapped modal); contact.tsx lists social links with a copy-to-clipboard email helper.
tour.languageLesson: The section-map indirection means portfolio.tsx never imports section components directly — it resolves them by key, keeping the hub decoupled from content and making sections swappable.

tour.title: Context Providers: run() and the Fragment Explosion
tour.description: Two React context providers glue the terminal to the rest of the page. run-command.tsx exposes a run() callback through context so deep components (like about.tsx's command links) can execute terminal commands without prop drilling. fragment-explosion.tsx exposes a fragment-explosion signal backed by the use-fragment-explosion hook, which shatters an element's text into animated per-letter fragments through flash/burst/falling phases — the 'shatter/crash' easter egg from the README, wired in at the very top of the tree by page.tsx.
tour.languageLesson: Context providers are the idiomatic way to share imperative capabilities (run a command, trigger an explosion) across a component tree without threading callbacks through every prop.

tour.title: Easter Eggs: Effects and the Hooks That Drive Them
tour.description: The retro-computing character comes from hidden triggers. use-easter-eggs.ts orchestrates timed visual effects (matrix rain, glitch, upside-down, DVD bounce) and cancels pending timers on rapid re-trigger. use-reduced-motion.ts is an SSR-safe hook tracking the prefers-reduced-motion media query so effects respect accessibility. The effects themselves are canvas/DOM animations: matrix-rain.tsx (multi-script glyph rain), glitch-banner.tsx (character-by-character scramble, fed by hire-me-art.ts figlet rows), dvd-overlay.tsx (DVD-screensaver physics), and ascii-background.tsx (a domain-warped noise field).
tour.languageLesson: Timing bugs in effects come from uncleared timers — this code cancels pending timers on re-trigger and unmount (see the rapid and matrix tests), the standard fix for 'phantom' animations.

tour.title: The Lab: Canvas Physics Experiments
tour.description: The `lab` command opens a sandbox of playful, standalone canvas experiments. lab.tsx is the terminal-styled host that staggers line reveals around two experiments: gravity-well.tsx simulates particles orbiting a pointer-dragged attractor with Keplerian velocities, and black-hole.tsx ray-marches an ASCII accretion disk around an event horizon with gravitational lensing. lib/canvas-utils.ts is their shared helper: it resolves any CSS custom property to an sRGB tuple via a 1x1 canvas readback, so the lab art matches the active theme palette.
tour.languageLesson: Canvas readback (drawing a color to a 1x1 canvas and reading pixels) is a reliable way to convert CSS color strings like var(--primary) into numeric RGB for WebGL/canvas math.

tour.title: Testing: Vitest, Testing Library, and the Command Pipeline
tour.description: The project treats the terminal as a serious piece of software. vitest.config.ts runs tests in jsdom with the @ alias mapped to the project root; vitest.setup.ts registers @testing-library/jest-dom matchers. commands.test.ts asserts getStaticResponse output and — notably — that secret commands are not exposed in tab completion; portfolio.test.tsx drives the real UI with a run() helper that types into the terminal and asserts the rendered result. Tests are co-located with their components throughout the repo.
tour.languageLesson: jsdom + Testing Library test 'what the user sees': render the real component, type real input, assert real output — the same loop a browser test would, without a browser.

tour.title: Deploy: GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages
tour.description: The whole point of a static export is painless hosting. deploy.yml runs npm ci + npm run build on push to main (or manual dispatch), uploads the ./out artifact, and deploys it to GitHub Pages via actions/deploy-pages with pages/id-token permissions and a concurrency guard. The static assets make the export serve correctly: public/.nojekyll prevents Jekyll from processing the site, public/CNAME points the custom domain at the pages host, public/icon.svg is the terminal-green favicon, and public/status.json feeds the availability status shown in the terminal.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Pages deployment via OIDC (pages/id-token) avoids storing a deploy token — the workflow requests a short-lived token from the Pages environment at runtime.

tour.title: Agent-Facing Guidance: Rules and Skills
tour.description: Finally, the project documents how it wants to be modified. CLAUDE.md is the commit contract: one logical change per commit, imperative Conventional Commits subjects, no 'and', and a fixed author identity. .claude/rules/no-casual-rule-rewrites.md declares that rule files are durable and must not be rewritten without a clear reason. .claude/skills/blog-site-style/SKILL.md instructs agents to preserve the terminal-portfolio aesthetic (dark green + amber palette) when making changes. These files keep future contributors — human or AI — consistent with the README's vision.
tour.languageLesson: Treating commit conventions and design rules as machine-readable repo files turns 'please keep the style consistent' into an enforceable, checkable contract.
